AGENCY:

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
The Commission hereby gives notice that it has instituted reviews pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, to determine whether revocation of the antidumping duty orders on polyester textured yarn from Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury. Pursuant to the Act, interested parties are requested to respond to this notice by submitting the information specified below to the Commission.
DATES:
Instituted November 2, 2026. To be assured of consideration, the deadline for responses is December 2, 2026. Comments on the adequacy of responses may be filed with the Commission by January 12, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Judson Monson (202-205-3314), Office of Investigations, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436. Hearing-impaired persons can obtain information on this matter by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on 202-205-1810. Persons with mobility impairments who will need special assistance in gaining access to the Commission should contact the Office of the Secretary at 202-205-2000. General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server (
https://www.usitc.gov). The public record for this proceeding may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background.
—On December 14, 2021, the Department of Commerce (“Commerce”) issued antidumping duty orders on imports of polyester textured yarn from Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam (86 FR 71031). The Commission is conducting reviews pursuant to section 751(c) of the Act, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1675(c)), to determine whether revocation of the orders would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury to the domestic industry within a reasonably foreseeable time. Provisions concerning the conduct of this proceeding may be found in the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure at 19 CFR part 201, subparts A and B, and 19 CFR part 207, subparts A and F. The Commission will assess the adequacy of interested party responses to this notice of institution to determine whether to conduct full or expedited reviews. The Commission's determinations in any expedited reviews will be based on the facts available, which may include information provided in response to this notice.
Definitions.
—The following definitions apply to these reviews:
(1)
Subject Merchandise
is the class or kind of merchandise that is within the scope of the five-year reviews, as defined by Commerce.
(2) The
Subject Countries
in these reviews are Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam.
(3) The
Domestic Like Product
is the domestically produced product or products which are like, or in the absence of like, most similar in characteristics and uses with, the
Subject Merchandise.
In its original determinations, the Commission defined a single
Domestic Like Product
as polyester textured yarn, that is coextensive with the scope.
(4) The
Domestic Industry
is the U.S. producers as a whole of the
Domestic Like Product,
or those producers whose collective output of the
Domestic Like Product
constitutes a major proportion of the total domestic production of the product. In its original determinations, the Commission defined the
Domestic Industry
as all producers of polyester textured yarn.
(5) The
Order Date
is the date that the antidumping duty orders under review became effective. In these reviews, the
Order Date
is December 14, 2021.
(6) An
Importer
is any person or firm engaged, either directly or through a parent company or subsidiary, in importing the
Subject Merchandise
into the United States from a foreign manufacturer or through its selling agent.

AGENCY:
United States International Trade Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Commission hereby gives notice of the scheduling of expedited reviews pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930 (“the Act”) to determine whether revocation of the countervailing duty orders on utility scale wind towers from India and Malaysia and the antidumping duty orders on utility scale wind towers from India, Malaysia, and Spain would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury within a reasonably foreseeable time.
DATES:
October 5, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Laurel Schwartz—(202) 205-2398), Office of Investigations, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436. Hearing-impaired persons can obtain information on this matter by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on 202-205-1810. Persons with mobility impairments who will need special assistance in gaining access to the Commission should contact the Office of the Secretary at 202-205-2000. General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server (
https://www.usitc.gov). The public record for this proceeding may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background.
—On October 5, 2026, the Commission determined that the domestic interested party group response to its notice of institution (91 FR 40578, July 2, 2026) of the subject five-year reviews was adequate and that the domestic interested party group response was inadequate. The Commission did not find any other circumstances that would warrant conducting full reviews.[1]
Accordingly, the Commission determined that it would conduct expedited reviews pursuant to section 751(c)(3) of the Act (19 U.S.C. 1675(c)(3)).[2]
For further information concerning the conduct of these reviews and rules of general application, consult the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, part 201, subparts A and B (19 CFR part 201), and part 207, subparts A, D, E, and F (19 CFR part 207).
Staff report.
—A staff report containing information concerning the subject matter of the reviews has been placed in the nonpublic record, and will be made available to persons on the Administrative Protective Order service list for these reviews on January 7, 2027. A public version will be issued thereafter, pursuant to § 207.62(d)(4) of the Commission's rules.
Written submissions.
—As provided in § 207.62(d) of the Commission's rules, interested parties that are parties to the reviews and that have provided individually adequate responses to the notice of institution,[3]
and any party other than an interested party to the reviews may file written comments with the Secretary on what determination the Commission should reach in the reviews. Comments are due on or before January 14, 2027 and may not contain
( printed page 68971)
new factual information. Any person that is neither a party to the five-year reviews nor an interested party may submit a brief written statement (which shall not contain any new factual information) pertinent to the reviews by January 14, 2027. However, should the Department of Commerce (“Commerce”) extend the time limit for its completion of the final results of its reviews, the deadline for comments (which may not contain new factual information) on Commerce's final results is three business days after the issuance of Commerce's results. If comments contain business proprietary information (BPI), they must conform with the requirements of §§ 201.6, 207.3, and 207.7 of the Commission's rules. The Commission's
Handbook on Filing Procedures, available on the Commission's website at
https://www.usitc.gov/documents/handbook_on_filing_procedures.pdf, elaborates upon the Commission's procedures with respect to filings.
In accordance with §§ 201.16(c) and 207.3 of the rules, each document filed by a party to the reviews must be served on all other parties to the reviews (as identified by either the public or BPI service list), and a certificate of service must be timely filed. The Secretary will not accept a document for filing without a certificate of service.
Determination.
—The Commission has determined these reviews are extraordinarily complicated and therefore has determined to exercise its authority to extend the review period by up to 90 days pursuant to 19 U.S.C. 1675(c)(5)(B).
Authority:
These reviews are being conducted under authority of title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930; this notice is published pursuant to § 207.62 of the Commission's rules.
By order of the Commission.
Issued: October 28, 2026.
Lisa Barton,
Secretary to the Commission.
Footnotes
1.
A record of the Commissioners' votes, the Commission's statement on adequacy, and any individual Commissioner's statements will be available from the Office of the Secretary and at the Commission's website.
3.
The Commission has found the response submitted on behalf of the Wind Tower Trade Coalition and Ventower Industries LLC to be individually adequate. Comments from other interested parties will not be accepted (
see19 CFR 207.62(d)(2)).

articles.title: President Directs Section 232 Negotiations on Robotics and Industrial Machinery Imports, Defers Tariffs or Quotas - Thompson Hine
articles.summary: President Directs Section 232 Negotiations on Robotics and Industrial Machinery Imports, Defers Tariffs or Quotas  Thompson Hine
articles.full_text:
On October 28, 2026, President Trump issued a proclamation titled “Adjusting Imports of Robotics, Industrial Machinery, and Their Parts and Components into the United States,” directing the Secretary of Commerce and the United States Trade Representative (USTR) to jointly pursue negotiations with trading partners to address the national security threat posed by these imports. Rather than imposing tariffs or quotas now, the proclamation makes negotiated agreements the initial remedy.
The action follows a Commerce investigation initiated under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1862) (see Update of September 25, 2025). The Secretary found that robotics, industrial machinery, and their parts and components “are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States,” and the President concurred.
According to the proclamation, the Secretary found that:
- robotics and industrial machinery support production of defense systems such as aircraft, tanks, ships, weapons, and munitions;
- robotics and industrial machines are crucial to the United States’ critical infrastructure sectors and other key aspects of the United States economy;
- the United States relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery and their components, and the value of those imports has increased over the last decade;
- robotics and machinery from “certain foreign entities pose unique security and safety risks,” including cybersecurity vulnerabilities, because they routinely process and store sensitive data; and
- domestic industry does not produce enough of these products to meet national security needs.
The proclamation states that, “[d]epending on the status or outcome of such negotiations,” the President “may consider alternative remedies in the future, including imposing or modifying tariffs, duties, quotas, and fees; and establishing a program to incentivize new investment in United States production of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as their parts and components.” It also notes that, under 19 U.S.C. 1862(c)(3)(A), the President may take other actions “to adjust imports to eliminate the threat that the imported article poses to the national security” if an agreement is not entered into within 180 days, is not being carried out, or is ineffective.
The Secretary and USTR must update the President on the negotiations within 180 days of the date of the proclamation. Importers and manufacturers that rely on imported robotics and industrial machinery should consider monitoring these negotiations, as tariffs, quotas, fees, or other actions remain possible.
Notably, the security concerns regarding foreign-sourced robotics echo recent Federal Communications Commission (FCC) actions adding advanced robotic devices and power inverters to the FCC Covered List (see Update of August 4, 2026; see also Update of August 26, 2026).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Each year during the anniversary month of the publication of an antidumping duty (AD) or countervailing duty (CVD) order, finding, or suspended investigation, an interested party, as defined in section 771(9) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as
( printed page 68937)
amended (the Act), may request, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213, that the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) conduct an administrative review of that AD or CVD order, finding, or suspended investigation.
All deadlines for the submission of comments or actions by Commerce discussed below refer to the number of calendar days from the applicable starting date.
Commerce asks that requests for review of multiple companies include an appendix listing, in alphabetical order, the company names for which a review is requested.
See infra
for additional details regarding this request.
Respondent Selection
In the event Commerce limits the number of respondents for individual examination for administrative reviews initiated pursuant to requests made for the orders identified below, Commerce intends to select respondents based on U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) data for U.S. imports during the period of review (POR). We intend to release the CBP data under administrative protective order (APO) to all parties having an APO within five days of publication of the initiation notice and to make our decision regarding respondent selection within 35 days of publication of the initiation
Federal Register
notice. Therefore, we encourage all parties interested in commenting on respondent selection to submit their APO applications on the date of publication of the initiation notice, or as soon thereafter as possible. Commerce invites comments regarding the CBP data and respondent selection within five days of placement of the CBP data on the record of the review.
In the event Commerce decides it is necessary to limit individual examination of respondents and conduct respondent selection under section 777A(c)(2) of the Act:
1. In general, Commerce finds that determinations concerning whether particular companies should be “collapsed” (
i.e.,
treated as a single entity for purposes of calculating AD rates) require a substantial amount of detailed information and analysis, which often require follow-up questions and analysis. Accordingly, Commerce will not conduct collapsing analyses at the respondent selection phase of a review and will not collapse companies at the respondent selection phase unless there has been a determination to collapse certain companies in a previous segment of this AD proceeding (
i.e.,
investigation, administrative review, new shipper review, or changed circumstances review).
2. For any company subject to a review, if Commerce determined, or continued to treat, that company as collapsed with others, Commerce will assume that such companies continue to operate in the same manner and will collapse them for respondent selection purposes. Otherwise, Commerce will not collapse companies for purposes of respondent selection.
3. Parties are requested to: (a) identify which companies subject to review previously were collapsed; and (b) provide a citation to the proceeding in which they were collapsed.
4. Further, if companies are requested to complete a Quantity and Value Questionnaire for purposes of respondent selection, in general, each company must report volume and value data separately for itself. Parties should not include data for any other party, even if they believe they should be treated as a single entity with that other party. If a company was collapsed with another company or companies in the most recently completed segment of a proceeding where Commerce considered collapsing that entity, complete quantity and value data for that collapsed entity must be submitted.

Section 504 of the Trade Preferences Extension Act of 2015 amended the Act by adding the concept of particular market situation (PMS) for purposes of constructed value under section 773(e) of the Act.[1]
Section 773(e) of the Act states that “if a particular market situation exists such that the cost of materials and fabrication or other processing of any kind does not accurately reflect the cost of production in the ordinary course of trade, the administering authority may use another calculation methodology under this subtitle or any other calculation methodology.” When an interested party submits a PMS allegation, pursuant to section 773(e) of the Act, Commerce will respond to such a submission consistent with 19 CFR 351.301(c)(2)(v). If Commerce finds that a PMS exists under section 773(e) of the Act, then it will modify its dumping calculations appropriately.

articles.title: Zero-tariff boosts India’s imports of electronic components from Vietnam - Tuoi Tre News | The News Gateway to Vietnam
articles.summary: Zero-tariff boosts India’s imports of electronic components from Vietnam  Tuoi Tre News | The News Gateway to Vietnam

source_detail.name: Tuoi Tre News | The News Gateway to Vietnam

articles.full_text:
According to India's BusinessLine, electronics manufacturers, particularly makers of smartphones and true wireless stereo (TWS) earbuds, have stepped up imports from Vietnam as memory chip prices have nearly quintupled over the past year.
Industry sources expect the trend to continue gaining momentum this year.
Citing Indian government data, BusinessLine reported that the value of India’s imports of electronic goods from Vietnam reached US$5.36 billion in fiscal year 2025-26, up 9.5 percent from approximately $4.9 billion a year earlier.
Imports of these products had previously reached $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2023-24, up 16.1 percent from $3.88 billion in fiscal year 2022-23.
According to several industry sources, many companies have taken advantage of zero import duties on eligible goods from Vietnam to bring in large volumes of smartphone components and other electronic products over the past year.
A veteran industry expert said components such as screens, camera modules and even Bluetooth earphones were being imported from Vietnam at zero tariffs.
The expert said most importers were Chinese companies with manufacturing or assembly facilities in India. Rather than importing directly from China, these businesses are increasingly sourcing components from Vietnam.
Some companies have also been importing TWS earbuds directly from Vietnam because doing so is significantly cheaper than manufacturing them in India. Others have even opted to build factories in Vietnam instead of India.
Under the ASEAN-India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA), electronic goods imported from Vietnam may qualify for preferential tariffs if they meet rules of origin requirements and are accompanied by valid certificates of origin (C/Os).
This mechanism allows eligible products to enjoy preferential rates instead of most-favored-nation (MFN) tariffs, which generally range from 0 to 20 percent for most electronic products.
Investing in screen manufacturing facilities in India under production incentive schemes may qualify companies for incentives of 4 percent. By contrast, importing the same products from Vietnam at zero tariffs could offer higher profit margins without requiring companies to invest in factories in India.
Vietnam's electronics exports post strong growth
According to figures from the General Department of Vietnam Customs released by the Ministry of Industry and Trade on Saturday, as of October 15, 2026, exports of computers, electronic products and components, as well as phones and components, had reached $189.65 billion, accounting for around 40 percent of Vietnam's total export turnover.
Exports of computers, electronic products and components alone amounted to $135.31 billion, up 65.2 percent year on year.

The Commission hereby gives notice that it has instituted a review pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, to determine whether revocation of the antidumping duty order on potassium permanganate from China would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background.
—On January 31, 1984, the Department of Commerce (“Commerce”) issued an antidumping duty order on imports of potassium permanganate from China (49 FR 3897).

The Commission is now conducting a sixth review pursuant to section 751(c) of the Act, as amended (19 U.

Provisions concerning the conduct of this proceeding may be found in the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure at 19 CFR part 201, subparts A and B, and 19 CFR part 207, subparts A and F.
The Commission will assess the adequacy of interested party responses to this notice of institution to determine whether to conduct a full or expedited review.
The Commission's determination in any expedited review will be based on the facts available, which may include information provided in response to this notice.

Definitions.
—The following definitions apply to this review:
(1)
Subject Merchandise
is the class or kind of merchandise that is within the scope of the five-year review, as defined by Commerce.
(2) The

(3) The

articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
                    DATES:
Applicable November 2, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
                    On August 4, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) initiated less-than-fair-value (LTFV) investigations of imports of welded stainless line and pressure pipe (welded stainless pipe) from India, Türkiye, and the UAE.[] 
                    
                     Currently, the preliminary determinations are due no later than December 22, 2026.
                
Postponement of Preliminary Determinations
Section 733(b)(1)(A) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), requires Commerce to issue the preliminary determination in an LTFV investigation within 140 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation. However, section 733(c)(1)(A)(b)(1) of the Act permits Commerce to postpone the preliminary determination until no later than 190 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation if: (A) the petitioner makes a timely request for a postponement; or (B) Commerce concludes that the parties concerned are cooperating, that the investigation is extraordinarily complicated, and that additional time is necessary to make a preliminary determination. Under 19 CFR 351.205(e), the petitioner must submit a request for postponement 25 days or more before the scheduled date of the preliminary determination and must state the reasons for the request. Commerce will grant the request unless it finds compelling reasons to deny the request.
                    On October 23, 2026, the petitioners [] 
                    
                     submitted a timely request that Commerce postpone the preliminary determinations in these LTFV investigations.[] 
                    
                     The petitioners stated that they request postponement “given the size and complexity of these investigations, the number of participating respondents, and the numerous extensions of time received by respondents to submit responses to Commerce's initial questionnaire. Postponement of the preliminary determinations will allow the petitioners adequate time to analyze and comment on the respondents' questionnaire responses and develop a comprehensive record in these investigations that the petitioners can then comment on in advance of Commerce's preliminary determinations.” [] 
                    
                
                    For the reasons stated above and because there are no compelling reasons to deny the request, Commerce, in accordance with section 733(c)(1)(A) of the Act, is postponing the deadline for the preliminary determinations by 50 days (
                    i.e.,
                     190 days after the date on which these investigations were initiated). As a result, Commerce will issue its preliminary determinations no later than February 10, 2027. In accordance with section 735(a)(1) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.210(b)(1), the deadline for the final determinations of these investigations will continue to be 75 days after the date of the preliminary determinations, unless postponed at a later date.
                
This notice is issued and published pursuant to section 733(c)(2) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.205(f)(1).
                    Dated: October 28, 2026.
Scot Fullerton,
Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Operations.

articles.full_text:
This paper shows retailers increase prices in response to organized retail crime. We match store-level crime data to scanner data from the universe of transactions for cannabis retailers in Washington state. Using quasi-experimental variation from robberies and burglaries, we find a 1.7–1.8 percent price increase at victimized stores and nearby competitors. This rise is not driven by short-to-medium-term demand changes but is consistent with crime-related cost shocks. Effects are larger for independent stores and less concentrated markets. We estimate crime imposes a 1 percent “hidden” unit tax on affected stores, implying $30.7 million in additional social costs, primarily borne by consumers.
That is from a newly published paper, AEJ: Economic Policy, by Carl Hase and Johannes Kasinger.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that HD Hyundai Electric Co., Ltd. (Hyundai) and Iljin Electric Co., Ltd (Iljin) did not make sales of subject merchandise at less than normal value (NV) during the period of review (POR), August 1, 2024, through July 31, 2025. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 25, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), we initiated an administrative review of the antidumping duty order on large power transformers from the Republic of Korea (Korea).[1]
On January 29, 2026, Commerce selected Hyundai and Iljin as the mandatory respondents in this review.[2]
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.[3]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.[4]
On July 9, 2026, we extended the preliminary results of this review to no later than October 30, 2026.[5]
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[6]
A list of the topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is attached as an appendix to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS). ACCESS is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.

The merchandise subject to the

is large power transformers from Korea. For a complete description of the scope of the

Methodology
Commerce is conducting this review in accordance with section 751(a) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). Constructed export prices have been calculated in accordance with section 772 of the Act. NV is calculated in accordance with section 773 of the Act. For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rate for Non-Individually Examined Companies
The Act and Commerce's regulations do not address the establishment of a rate to apply to companies not selected for individual examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(c)(2) of the Act. Generally, Commerce looks to section 735(c)(5) of the Act, which provides instructions for calculating the all-others rate in a market economy investigation, for guidance when calculating the rate for companies which were not selected for individual examination in an administrative review.
Under section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act, the all-others rate is normally an amount equal to the weighted average of the estimated weighted-average dumping margins established for exporters and producers individually investigated, excluding any rates that are zero,
de minimis
(
i.e.,

AGENCY:

                    ACTION:
Notice; withdrawal.
                    SUMMARY:
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) is issuing this notice to advise Federal, State, local governmental agencies, and the public and other concerned stakeholders that USACE is withdrawing the Notice of Intent (NOI) for the preparation of an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) as part of the Port of Iberia (also referred to as `the Port' or `Iberia Port'), Louisiana navigation feasibility study. Since publication of the NOI, study conditions have changed; the USACE has determined that an Environmental Assessment (EA) rather than an EIS is the appropriate level of environmental documentation.
                    DATES:
                        The NOI to prepare an EIS published in the 
                        Federal Register
                         on October 31, 2002 (67 FR 66388), is withdrawn as of November 2, 2026.
                    
                    ADDRESSES:
U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, New Orleans; 7400 Leake Ave., New Orleans, Louisiana 70118.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 431 (Iberia Port, Louisiana) of the Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) of 2000 (Pub. L. 106-541) authorized “a study to determine the feasibility of carrying out a project for navigation, Iberia Port, Louisiana.” A final Feasibility Report and EIS were completed in 2006; however, a Record of Decision for the EIS was not signed. The project was subsequently authorized under Section 1001(25) of the WRDA 2007, as amended by Section 6004(a)(7) of the Water Resources Reform and Development Act of 2014.
                    USACE has since assessed the environmental impacts of the proposed action and determined that there would be no significant adverse impact(s) on the human and natural environment. Unavoidable impacts to wetlands will be fully mitigated; and because forecasted impacts from the proposed action can be fully mitigated, significant adverse effects are no longer a concern, an EIS is not warranted. The USACE will notify the public in advance of the availability of EA #611 and draft Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) through public notice. A copy of the signed FONSI will be made available for viewing and download on the project website at: 
                    https://www.mvn.usace.army.mil/About/Projects/Port-of-Iberia/.
                     Any future proposed federal action(s) related to the study, or authorized project if authorized, will comply with the requirements of the NEPA of 1969, as amended (42 U.S.C. 4321 
                    et seq.), the Department of War NEPA Implementing Procedures (September 3, 2026), and other related environmental review requirements.
                
                    James A. Bodron,
Programs Director, Mississippi Valley Division.

AGENCY:
Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, USDA.
                    ACTION:
Revision to and extension of approval of an information collection; comment request.
                    SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, this notice announces the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service's intention to request a revision to and extension of approval of an information collection associated with the operations and reporting system for cooperative wildlife damage management programs.
                    DATES:
We will consider all comments that we receive on or before January 4, 2027.
                    ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by either of the following methods:
- Federal eRulemaking Portal:
                         Go to 
                        www.regulations.gov.
                         Enter APHIS-2026-0892 in the Search field. Select the Documents tab, then select the Comment button in the list of documents.
                    
- Postal Mail/Commercial Delivery:
                         Please send one copy of your comment to Docket No. APHIS-2026-0892, Regulatory Analysis and Development, PPD, APHIS, 5601 Sunnyside Ave., #AP760, Beltsville, MD 20705.
                    
                        Supporting documents and any comments we receive on this docket may be viewed at 
                        www.regulations.gov
                         or in our reading room, which is in room 1620 of the USDA South Building, 14th Street and Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC. Normal reading room hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, except holidays. To be sure someone is there to help you, please call (202) 799-7039 before coming.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    Title:
                     Operations and Reporting System.
                
                    OMB Control Number:
                     0579-0335.
                
                    Type of Request:
                     Revision to and extension of approval of an information collection.
                
                    Abstract:
                     The Secretary of Agriculture is authorized under Section 426 of the Act of March 2, 1931, as amended (7 U.S.C. 8351-8354; 46 Stat. 1468), to conduct a program of wildlife services with respect to injurious animal species. Large populations of aggressive wildlife species, if left unmanaged, may cause tremendous amounts of damage to crops, livestock herds, and private property within the United States. Without mitigation, the damage could result in severe economic losses for agricultural businesses and private property owners. The Act authorizes the Secretary to take any action he considers necessary for the control of nuisance mammals and birds and those mammal and bird species that are reservoirs for zoonotic diseases.
                
The United States Department of Agriculture, Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), Wildlife Services (WS), is responsible for assisting the public with mitigating wildlife damage. WS provides advice or enters into agreements with State and local jurisdictions, Tribes, public and private agencies, organizations, institutions, and individuals to provide its services. Through its technical assistance approach, WS offers advice through telephone or onsite consultations, training sessions, demonstration projects, and other means. Mitigation activities are then performed by the requester. WS also provides a cooperative direct control approach where goods, services, and expertise are provided on a cost reimbursable basis. WS collects only information needed to determine appropriate courses of action for providing effective services. Information is used by the agency to:
- Identify cooperators appropriately;
- Identify lands on which WS personnel will work;
- Differentiate between cooperators (i.e.,
                     property owners, land managers, or resource owners) who request assistance to manage damage caused by wildlife;
                
- Identify the land areas on which wildlife damage management activities would be conducted;
- Identify the relationship between resources or property, WS' protection of such resources or property, and the damage caused by wildlife;
- Determine the methods or damage management activities to deal with the damage;
- Establish a record that a cooperative agreement has been entered into with a cooperator;
- Document that permission has been obtained from landowners to go on the cooperator's property;
- Record wildlife damage occurrences on cooperator's property and steps to address them;
- Record occurrences which may have affected non-target species or humans during, or related to, WS project actions; and
- Determine satisfaction with service to help WS evaluate, modify, and improve its programs.
Information collection activities include work initiation documents, assistance requests, protected resource queries, project reports, order forms and sales records, equipment issuances, migratory bird damage reports, reports of injury or death to non-target animals, accident reports, pilot proficiency reviews, and invoice transmittals.
We are asking the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to approve our use of these information collection activities for an additional 3 years. APHIS has renamed this information collection to Operations and Reporting System, the information collection was formerly known as National Management Information System.
The purpose of this notice is to solicit comments from the public (as well as affected agencies) concerning our information collection. These comments will help us:
(1) Evaluate whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
(2) Evaluate the accuracy of our estimate of the burden of the collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
(3) Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
                    (4) Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, through use, as appropriate, of automated, electronic, mechanical, and other collection technologies; 
                    e.g.,
                     permitting electronic submission of responses.
                
                    Estimate of burden:
                     The public burden for this collection of information is estimated to average 0.042 hours per response.
                
                    Respondents:
                     State, local, and Tribal governments; businesses, not-for-profits, and other public sector organizations; and individuals who request services from WS or engage in wildlife damage management projects with WS.
                
                    Estimated annual number of respondents:
                     77,712.
                
                    Estimated annual number of responses per respondent:
                     1.
                
                    Estimated annual number of responses:
                     86,274.
                
                    Estimated total annual burden on respondents:
                     3,608 hours. (Due to averaging, the total annual burden hours may not equal the product of the annual number of responses multiplied by the reporting burden per response.)
                
All responses to this notice will be summarized and included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will also become a matter of public record.
                    Done in Washington, DC, this 19th day of October 2026.
Kelly Moore,
Administrator, Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.

This document announces that OMB approved the information collection requirements in 47 CFR 27.1412(e) on September 21, 2026. Synopsis
As required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3507), the Commission is notifying the public that it received final OMB approval on September 21, 2026, for the information collection requirements contained in 47 CFR 27.1412(e). Under 5 CFR part 1320, an agency may not conduct or sponsor a collection of information unless it displays a current, valid OMB Control Number.
No person shall be subject to any penalty for failing to comply with a collection of information subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act that does not display a current, valid OMB Control Number. The OMB Control Number for this information collection is 3060-1272. The foregoing notice is required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, Public Law 104-13, October 1, 1995, and 44 U.S.C. 3507.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of information collection, request for comment.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Commerce, in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, invites the general public and other Federal agencies to comment on proposed, and continuing information collections, which helps us assess the impact of our information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. The purpose of this notice is to allow for 60 days of public comment on the revision of the American Community Survey and the Puerto Rico Community Survey, prior to the submission of the information collection request (ICR) to OMB for approval.
DATES:
To ensure consideration, comments regarding this proposed information collection must be received on or before January 4, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
Interested persons are invited to submit written comments by email to
acso.pra@census.gov.
Please reference the American Community Survey and the Puerto Rico Community Survey in the subject line of your comments. You may also submit comments, identified by Docket Number USBC-2026-0760 to the Federal e-Rulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov.
Click the “Comment” icon, complete the required fields, and enter or attach your comments. All comments received are part of the public record. No comments will be posted to
https://www.regulations.gov
for public viewing until after the comment period has closed. Comments will generally be posted without change. All Personally Identifiable Information (for example, name and address) voluntarily submitted by the commenter may be publicly accessible. Do not submit Confidential Business Information or otherwise sensitive or protected information. You may submit attachments to electronic comments in Microsoft Word, Excel, or Adobe PDF file formats.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Requests for additional information or specific questions related to collection activities should be directed to Nicole Butler, U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey Office, 301-763-3928,
nicole.butler@census.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Abstract
The U.S. Census Bureau seeks a revision for the American Community Survey (ACS) and the Puerto Rico Community Survey (PRCS). The ACS program provides information every year on over 40 topics—giving communities, businesses, and governments the current information they need about our nation and its people. ACS data also help inform how trillions of dollars in federal funds are distributed each year.
The ACS content is designed to serve the data needs of federal government agencies and, in addition, provides a rich source of local area information useful to a wide variety of data users, including state and local governments, universities, and private businesses. The ACS is part of the Decennial Census Program. Historically, the decennial census sampled addresses to complete a “long form,” which collected detailed population and housing characteristics once a decade whereas a majority of addresses were asked to a complete a “short form” which collected basic demographic information. The demand for current, nationally consistent data from a wide variety of data users led federal government policymakers to consider the feasibility of collecting detailed population and housing data continuously throughout the decade. This led the Census Bureau to plan the ACS as a replacement for the “long form.”
Since its implementation in 2005, the ACS has collected detailed social, economic, housing, and demographic data on more than 40 topics on an ongoing basis, providing more timely data than was previously possible. Every question on the ACS must meet an explicit need from one or more federal agencies. Constraining the content of the ACS was, and still is, critical because of the mandatory reporting requirement and because doing so reduces the burden on the American people. The Census Bureau periodically reviews the questions on the ACS to ensure that existing content serves the data needs of federal agencies and to evaluate new question proposals from federal agencies. The Census Bureau classifies federal agency uses of the ACS as mandatory, required, programmatic, or operational as follows:
There is a current federal law calling for the use of decennial census
( printed page 68929)
data for a particular federal program (mandatory).
A federal law (or implementing regulation) clearly requires the use of specific data, and the decennial census was the historical or only source, or case law requirements imposed by the U.S. federal court system need the data (required).
A federal agency indicated they use the data (or need data on a topic) but there is no explicit requirement for the use of the data, as explained for mandatory or required purposes (programmatic).
The data are necessary to administer the survey, such as phone numbers (operational).
Only uses identified as mandatory, required, or operational result in questions on the ACS. Programmatic uses alone do not result in questions being added to the ACS.
In 2026, the Census Bureau conducted a content review of the ACS to ensure that every question on the ACS is legally justified and has a federal use. Over 60 federal agencies provided input on their use of ACS data, representing 17 independent agencies and all but three cabinet departments. The MCAI states that an occurrence was reported where, during the final testing of a BRP-Rotax Model 916i engine on the production line, oil leakage was found in the area of the turbocharger valve housing. This condition, if not detected and corrected, could result in oil leakage during engine operation, smoke generation, engine compartment fire, an in-flight engine shutdown, and possible loss of control of the airplane.

articles.full_text:
Bryan Caplan:
It seems like you and other AIs are bad Bayesians. When presented with counterevidence, you should move toward or against the presenter with roughly equal probability. It depends on whether the argument was better or worse than expected. In fact, you seem to either move toward the speaker or just not change.
ChatGPT:
I think you’ve identified a genuine and important failure mode in AI reasoning: LLMs tend to treat a plausible counterargument as evidence in favor of its conclusion, rather than comparing the counterargument to what they should have expected to hear.
Your Bayesian point is correct, with one qualification: there’s no general theorem that updating toward and away from a speaker should happen with equal probability. But under appropriate calibration assumptions, both directions should occur, and an argument that’s weaker than expected should cause a negative update—even if the argument is perfectly valid as far as it goes.
Here is the full dialogue.  But will they try to fix this?  Should they try to fix this?  Can you undo this with good enough prompting?  The scope and limits of Bayesian are truly at stake here…

articles.full_text:
Education is widely recognized as the primary driver of human capital accumulation. However, policies designed to promote educational attainment often overlook students’ endogenous responses. This paper provides empirical evidence of the causal impact of relaxed academic standards on student effort and achievement. We find that academic leniency results in mechanical GPA increases, but significant reductions in effort among lower ability students based on lower attendance and lower numerical grades. These heterogeneous effects compound and exacerbate gaps in engagement and achievement throughout high school, ultimately worsening deficits in human capital accumulation as measured by ACT scores.
That is from a newly published paper, in AEJ: Economic Policy, by A. Brooks Bowden, Viviana Rodriguez, and Zach Weingarten.

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is amending its preliminary affirmative determination in the less-than-fair-value (LTFV) investigation of truck bed covers from the People's Republic of China (China) to correct for significant ministerial errors. The period of investigation is July 1, 2025, through December 31, 2025.
DATES:
Applicable November 2, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Christopher Maciuba or Jerry Xiao, AD/CVD Operations, Office II, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-0413 or (202) 482- 2273, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On October 1, 2026, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the
Preliminary Determination
of the less-than-fair-value investigation of truck bed covers from the People's Republic of China.[1]
On October 6, 2026, a non-selected respondent who had qualified for a separate rate, Ningbo Scarman International Trading Co., Ltd (Ningbo Scarman) timely alleged that Commerce made significant ministerial errors in assigning its estimated weighted-average dumping margins.[2]
Scope of the Investigation
The products covered by this investigation are truck bed covers from China. For a complete description of the scope of this investigation,
see
the
Preliminary Determination.[3]
Legal Framework
A ministerial error is defined as including “errors in addition, subtraction, or other arithmetic function, clerical error resulting from inaccurate copying, duplication, or the like, and any other similar type of unintentional error which {Commerce} considers ministerial.” [4]
A ministerial error is considered to be “significant” if its correction, either singly or in combination with other errors, would result in: (1) a change of at least f/ive absolute percentage points in, but not less than 25 percent of, the weighted-average dumping margin calculated in the preliminary determination; or (2) a difference between a weighted-average dumping margin of zero (or
de minimis) and a weighted-average dumping margin of greater than
de minimis
or vice versa.[5]
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.224(e), Commerce “will analyze any comments received and, if appropriate, correct any significant ministerial error by amending the preliminary determination.”
Analysis of Significant Ministerial Errors
In the
Preliminary Determination,
Commerce made a significant ministerial error within the meaning of section 735(e) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.224(f) and (g)(1) in incorrectly listing the producer when assigning a non-selected preliminary weighted-average dumping margin to Ningbo Scarman and its producer Ningbo Scarman Auto Parts Co., Ltd (Ningbo Auto Parts). Accordingly, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.224(e), Commerce is amending its
Preliminary Determination
to correct this error by correctly noting the producer/exporter chain as Ningbo Scarman/Ningbo Auto Parts chain, and assigning this chain the non-selected separate rate calculated in the
Preliminary Determination.[6]
For a detailed discussion of the alleged ministerial errors, as well as Commerce's analysis,
see
the Ministerial Error Memorandum.[7]
Amended Preliminary Determination
As a result of correcting this error specific to the producer/exporter combination discussed above, Commerce determines that the following estimated weighted-average dumping margin exists for the producer/exporter chain of Ningbo Scarman/Ningbo Auto Parts; no other changes have been made to any other producer/exporter combination as published in the
Preliminary Determination:

Disclosure
Because no changes were made to the margin calculations from the
Preliminary Determination
as a result of this ministerial error, there are no new calculations to disclose.
Amended Cash Deposits and Suspension of Liquidation
The collection of cash deposits and suspension of liquidation will be
( printed page 68944)
revised according to the rates calculated in this amended preliminary determination, in accordance with section 733(d) of the Act. Because we incorrectly identified this producer/exporter combination rate in the
Preliminary Determination,
this producer/exporter combination would have been suspended at the China-wide entity rate. Therefore, this notice corrects the Ningbo Scarman/Ningbo Auto Parts producer/exporter combination from the
Preliminary Determination,
to correct any inadvertent suspension at the incorrect cash deposit rate; the corrected producer/exporter combination identified above has a lower cash deposit rate than the China-wide entity rate that the producer and/or exporter may have been subject to since the
Preliminary Determination
published. As a result, the cash deposit instructions for this amended preliminary determination will be effective retroactively to October 1, 2026, the date of publication of the
Preliminary Determination.
We will also instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection to issue instructions for requesting a refund of the difference between the amount of cash deposits paid as a result of the application of the
Preliminary Determination
rates applied and the amount due as a result of this amended preliminary determination.
U.S. International Trade Commission Notification
In accordance with section 733(f) of the Act, we will notify the U.S. International Trade Commission of our amended preliminary determination.
Notification to Interested Parties
This notice is issued and published in accordance with sections 735(e) and 777(i)(1) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, and 19 CFR 351.224(e).

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This Notice publishes the Fiscal Year (FY) 2025 Cost of Incarceration Fee (COIF) for Federal inmates.
DATES:
This determination is effective as of November 2, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Office of General Counsel, Federal Bureau of Prisons, 320 First Street NW, Washington, DC 20534.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Whittington C. Wiman, Assistant General Counsel/Rules Administrator, Federal Bureau of Prisons, at the address above or at (202) 353-4885.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Pursuant to 28 CFR 0.96c and 28 CFR 505.2, this Notice publishes the FY 2025 COIF for Federal inmates. Title 28 of the Code of
( printed page 68985)
Federal Regulations, part 505, allows for assessment of a fee to cover the average cost of incarceration for Federal inmates. We calculate the COIF by dividing the number representing the Bureau of Prisons (Bureau) facilities' monetary obligation (excluding activation costs) by the number of inmate-days incurred for the fiscal year, and then by multiplying the quotient by the number of days in the fiscal year.
Based on FY 2025 data, the average annual COIF for a Federal inmate housed in a Bureau or non-Bureau facility in FY 2025 was $47,564 ($130.31 per day). The average annual COIF for a Federal inmate housed in a Residential Reentry Center for FY 2025 was $43,499 ($119.18 per day).
Sean D. Francisco,
Acting Assistant Director/General Counsel, Federal Bureau of Prisons.

This patent license covers two patent estates as shown above, namely the invention described in the E-017-2024 estate, and the invention described in the E-061-2022 estate. “Intramural substrates” are the crux of the clinical challenge addressed by the subject patent estates and the proposed field of use. Specifically, these intramural substrates are the electrically conducting and hard-to-reach arrhythmogenic tissue located within the depth of the myocardial wall—the mid-myocardium—rather than on the endocardial (inner) or epicardial (outer) surfaces. The inventions being exclusively licensed herein provide a catheter-based system and method to access these intramyocardium tissues, and a synchronous circumferential intramyocardial resynchronization and pacing (SCIRP) system intended to improve cardiac resynchronization therapy. Both of these inventions together provide a new and improved device, system and method to enable electrophysiologists to access and treat arrhythmogenic intramural substrates located within the ventricular myocardial wall, which currently is not systematized.
The invention described in E-017-2024, for which we have 3 provisional applications, 3 PCT applications, a pending U.

The system, referred to as VINTAGE (Ventricular Intramyocardial Navigation for Tachycardia Ablation Guided by Electrograms), principally uses a small flexible ablation microcatheter that tracks coaxially over a steerable, electrically insulated guidewire.
Proximal to the catheter tip are mapping electrodes and a conductive ablation electrodes with perforations that can elute irrigants directly into the surrounding myocardial tissue.
The physician navigates to the desired deep target using fluoroscopy, ultrasound, electroanatomic mapping and/or electrogram-based depth navigation (EDEN); once the ablation electrode reaches the target, irrigant is delivered through its openings and radiofrequency energy applied while irrigation continues, producing a controlled lesion in the abnormal tissue responsible for the arrhythmia.

AGENCY:
Office of Management and Budget.
                    ACTION:
Request for information; reopening of response period.
                    SUMMARY:
                        The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) published in the 
                        Federal Register
                         a request for information (RFI) regarding new and unused (idle) domestic, U.S.-based, and near shore production capabilities for Finished Dose Forms, Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients, and Key Starting Materials associated with the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (ASPR) 86 List of essential medicines. The RFI provided for a 30-day response period which closed on October 26, 2026. OMB has determined that reopening the comment period until November 27, 2026, is appropriate. This action will allow interested parties additional time to prepare information and responses.
                    
                    DATES:
The response period for the notice published on September 25, 2026 (91 FR 60983), regarding the RFI on Domestic and Near Shore Manufacturing of Essential Medicines on the ASPR 86 List, is reopened. Responses must be received on or before November 27, 2026.
                    ADDRESSES:
                        Responses must be submitted electronically through 
                        regulations.gov.
                         Mailed paper submissions will not be accepted, and electronic submissions received after the deadline may not be considered.
                    
                        Instructions:
                         Federal eRulemaking Portal: Go to 
                        www.regulations.gov
                         search “Domestic and Near Shore Manufacturing of Essential Medicines RFI” to submit your comments electronically. Information on how to use 
                        Regulations.gov,
                         including instructions for accessing agency documents, submitting comments, and viewing the docket, is available on the site under “FAQ” (
                        https://www.regulations.gov/faq). Should you choose to include proprietary information or confidential business information in your submission, please ensure you use appropriate markings and handling instructions to alert OMB as to the nature of information being submitted and maintain proper handling. Your response will be shared with other Federal agencies and entities.
                    
                        Privacy Act Statement:
                         OMB is issuing this request for information (RFI) pursuant to its authorities under 31 U.S.C. 501 
                        et seq.
                         Comments and commenter information are maintained under the OMB Public Input System of Records, OMB/INPUT/01. The system of records notice accessible at 88 FR 20913 (
                        https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/04/07/2023-07452/privacy-act-of-1974-system-of-records) includes a list of routine uses associated with the collection of this information.
                    
                        Disclaimer:
                         Participation in this RFI is strictly voluntary. OMB will use your feedback to inform sound decision-making on topics related to this RFI regarding potential government-wide actions to revitalize the domestic manufacturing base, create new opportunities for U.S. firms and workers, and position U.S. businesses to compete and lead globally in strategic industries. This announcement should not be construed as a commitment of any kind by the U.S. Government. The U.S. Government is in no way liable to pay for or reimburse any companies or entities that respond to this announcement. Nothing in this announcement constitutes an obligation on the part of the U.S. Government. A response to this RFI will not be viewed as a binding commitment to develop or pursue the project or ideas discussed.
                    
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    On September 25, 2026, OMB published in the 
                    Federal Register
                     an RFI soliciting responses on new and unused (idle) domestic, U.S.-based, and near shore production capabilities for Finished Dose Forms, Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients, and Key Starting Materials associated with the ASPR 86 List of essential medicines. The RFI stated that the response period would close on October 26, 2026. OMB has received requests to reopen the response period. Reopening the response period will allow interested parties additional time to prepare information and comments. Therefore, OMB is reopening the response period for the RFI until November 27, 2026.
                
                    Michael Stumo, 
Director, Made in America Office.

AGENCY:

Notice.
SUMMARY:
The National Park Service (NPS) announces its intent to extend, continue, and award concession contracts in accordance with 36 CFR part 51. To avoid interruptions in visitor services while new long-term contracts are developed and awarded, the NPS intends to extend certain existing contracts, continue others, and issue one temporary contract to maintain essential services until a new competitive contract becomes effective. These administrative actions ensure that visitor services remain uninterrupted across the affected park units.
DATES:
The National Park Service intends that the concession contract extensions, continuations, and temporary concession contract will be effective on the dates shown in the tables below, as applicable.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Kurt Rausch, Program Chief, Commercial Services Program, National Park Service, 1849 C Street NW, Mail Stop 2410, Washington, DC 20240; Telephone: 202-513-7156.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under 36 CFR 51.23 the NPS proposes to extend each contract listed in Table 1 until the date shown in the “Extension Expiration Date” column or until the effective date of a new contract, whichever comes first. The NPS has determined that the proposed extensions are necessary to avoid an interruption of visitor services and has taken all reasonable and appropriate steps to consider alternatives to avoid such an interruption. The extension of the existing contracts does not confer or affect any rights with respect to the award of new contracts.
The concession contracts listed in Table 2 below have been extended for the maximum time allowable under 36 CFR 51.23. Under the provisions of the existing contracts and pending the issuance of prospectuses and the completion of the public solicitation process to award new concession contracts, the NPS intends to continue the existing contracts until the date shown in the “Continuation Expiration Date” column or until the effective date of a new contract, whichever comes first. The continuation of the existing contracts does not confer or affect any rights with respect to the award of new concession contracts.
The NPS proposes awarding a temporary concession contract, in accordance with 36 CFR 51.24(a), to provide the visitor services currently provided under the contract listed in Table 3 below. The temporary contract will have a term not to exceed one year and will be awarded to a qualified person. The National Park Service anticipates that the temporary contract will be effective on the date shown in the “Effective Date” column. This notice is not a request for proposals.
The publication of this notice reflects the intent of the National Park Service but does not bind the National Park Service to extend, continue, or award any of the contracts listed below.

articles.full_text: The Department is issuing a final regulation that will require providers of pharmacy benefit management services and affiliated providers of brokerage and consulting services to disclose information about their compensation to fiduciaries of large, self-insured group health plans subject to the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA). Pharmacy spending is a major driver of overall healthcare costs for employers and is growing faster than medical and surgical spending. These disclosure requirements apply for purposes of ERISA's statutory prohibited transaction exemption for service arrangements under section 408(b)(2). These disclosures are needed so that fiduciaries can assess the reasonableness of contracts or arrangements with these service providers, including the reasonableness of the service providers' compensation. As directed in section 12 of President Trump's Executive Order 14273, Lowering Drug Prices by Once Again Putting Americans First, the Department is issuing this rule to improve employer health plan transparency into the direct and indirect compensation received by pharmacy benefit managers. This final rule will affect sponsors and other fiduciaries of large, self-insured group health plans and certain service providers to such plans.

AGENCY:
Forest Service, Agriculture (USDA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The United States Department of Agriculture (Department), Forest Service (Forest Service or Agency), this final rule will exempt administrative site leases from the regulations for special uses. The purpose of this deregulatory action is to better align Forest Service leasing activities with how leases are commonly legally defined to improve the feasibility of partnering with private developers and local municipalities for leasing and redeveloping administrative sites.
DATES:
The final rule is effective December 2, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Matthew Fountain, Sales and Leasing Program Manager, 202-205-1464 or
matthew.fountain1@usda.gov.
Individuals who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may call 711 to reach the Telecommunications Relay Service, then provide the phone number of the person named as a point of contact for further information.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background and Need
Administrative sites are land or property controlled by the Forest Service used or acquired for administrative purposes. The 2018 Farm Bill provides that the Secretary of Agriculture may lease an administrative site that is under the Secretary's jurisdiction under Public Law 115-334 Sec. 8623. The Forest Service Facility Realignment and Enhancement Act of 2005 (FSFREA), Public Law 109-54, also provides that the Forest Service may dispose of administrative sites by sale, lease, exchange, and other methods. The Administrative Site Leasing Program, which includes leasing administrative sites under both the Farm Bill and FSFREA authorities, was initially considered a special use authorization. This prevents the Agency from issuing leases that function as they are commonly legally defined, and the terms of the existing special use framework can discourage partnerships and investment. For example, special use authorization regulatory requirements, constrain the use of the leasehold interest as collateral for loans, limits assignment and transfer of the lease, and provides for unilateral termination of the authorization by the Forest Service. These requirements limit financing options and negatively impact the marketability of leasing projects.
Exempting administrative site leasing from special use regulation requirements will remove regulatory constraints incompatible with standard real estate leasing practices and reflect the unique statutory basis and long-term real property nature of these leases. Without this regulatory change, agency partners will continue to face challenges in obtaining the financing needed to pursue affordable housing and other projects under these authorities.
This final rule is intended to provide a consistent regulatory treatment of administrative site leases under both FSFREA and the 2018 Farm Bill by removing those leases from the special-use framework. Existing special use authorizations for administrative site leasing may remain in effect under their original terms or, at the authorized officer's discretion, be replaced, upon mutual agreement with the lessee, by a lease issued under the applicable statutory authority after satisfaction of all applicable requirements.
This final rule removes administrative site leasing authorized under section 8623 of the 2018 Farm Bill and FSFREA from the scope of 36 CFR part 251, subpart B. This change is expected to increase flexibility in how leasing projects are administered by separating incompatible processes that are unnecessary, irrelevant, or do not add value, while retaining processes necessary for legal sufficiency and public accountability. Additional programmatic guidance on administrative site leases can be found in Forest Service Manual 2750.
Summary of Comments and Responses
On May 6, 2026, the Forest Service published a proposed rule in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 24494) to exempt administrative site leases from the special use requirements in 36 CFR 251 to ensure compatible business practices are possible under the Administrative Site Leasing program. The agency received 25 comments; 8 were supportive of the proposed change and 17 were not. Comments were received from local governments, housing and public finance organizations, the general public and one Tribe. Several commenters supported the rule, emphasizing the need for affordable workforce housing in high-cost communities and explaining that current special-use requirements make financing difficult or impracticable for many projects. Those who opposed the proposed change, including the Osage Nation's Historic Preservation Office, generally expressed concern that the rule could facilitate privatization or disposal of National Forest System lands. The Department does not agree that the rule has that effect. The rule does not authorize land sales, change existing land-disposal authority, or exempt administrative-site leasing projects from National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), Archaeological Resources Protection Act (ARPA), National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), public notice, local-government consultation, or other applicable statutory requirements.
After reviewing all comments, the Department is adopting the proposed rule without change. The Department does not believe the concerns raised by commenters warrant changes to the rule text because the rule addresses only the regulatory treatment of administrative-site leases and does not alter statutory requirements or other legal requirements independent of subpart B that apply to future administrative-site leasing decisions.
A summary of substantive comments and responses is provided below.

Some commenters, especially those in housing finance, public finance, and local governments, support the rule because it could help address the need for affordable workforce housing, especially in high-cost communities. The current special

One commenter said their firm had reviewed multiple housing projects over five years, but lenders refused financing each time because the lease could not serve as loan collateral, the lease could not be assigned in case of default, and the Forest Service could end the lease unilaterally under the current regulatory framework.

AGENCY:
Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Criminal Law Technical Amendments Act of 2002 (“Technical Amendments Act”) became law on November 2, 2002, as part of the 21st Century Department of Justice Appropriations Authorization Act. The Technical Amendments Act amended sections 401(d), 402(c), and 403 of the Controlled Substances Act by replacing outmoded fine amounts with a reference to title 18 of the United States Code in each place that a specific fine amount had appeared. In this rulemaking, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) is amending its regulations to conform them to the statutory amendments made to the Controlled Substances Act by the Technical Amendments Act.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on November 2, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Heather E. Achbach, Regulatory Drafting and Policy Support Section, Diversion Control Division, Drug Enforcement Administration; Telephone: (571) 776-3882.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Legal Authority
The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) implements and enforces the Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970, often referred to as the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) and the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act, as amended.[1]
The CSA and its implementing regulations are designed to prevent, detect, and eliminate the diversion of controlled substances and listed chemicals into the illicit market while providing for the legitimate medical, scientific, research, and industrial needs of the United States. DEA publishes the implementing regulations for these statutes in 21 CFR parts 1300 through 1399.
On November 2, 2002, the Technical Amendments Act was enacted as part of the 21st Century Department of Justice Appropriations Authorization Act.[2]
The Technical Amendments Act amended sections 401(d), 402(c), and 403 of the CSA (21 U.S.C. 841(d), 842(c), and 843(d), respectively). Of particular relevance to this rulemaking, section 4002 of the Technical Amendments Act replaced the terms “of not more than $30,000” and “of not more than $60,000” with “under title 18, United States Code” each time the terms appeared in 21 U.S.C. 843(d). However, DEA regulations at 21 CFR 1301.17 continue to list “a fine of not more than $30,000” or a fine “not exceeding $30,000” as a possible penalty for providing false information on a registration application, intentionally misusing the affidavit procedure, and obtaining controlled substances through registration by fraudulent means.[3]
In this final rule, DEA is amending its regulations to conform to the amendments made to the CSA by the Technical Amendments Act. This rule replaces those terms with “under title 18, United States Code” each time the terms appear in 21 CFR 1301.17.

Administrative Procedure Act
An agency may find good cause to exempt a rule from certain provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA),[4]

DEA finds that there is good cause within the meaning of the APA to issue this amendment as a final rule without opportunity for public comment and with an immediate effective date.
This final rule amends DEA regulations only to the extent necessary to be consistent with current Federal law, as modified by the Technical Amendments Act. The Technical Amendments Act amended the penalty provisions of the CSA that DEA previously implemented in its regulations. Therefore, DEA is obligated to update those regulations. DEA is not exercising discretion with this final rule because this final rule merely amends the regulations to conform to the change to the CSA made by the Technical Amendments Act. Thus, publishing an NPRM or soliciting public comment is unnecessary.[5]
In addition, because the statutory changes addressed in this rule have already been in effect since November 2, 2002, DEA finds good cause exists to make this rule effective immediately upon publication.
